opus-5.5.text:
Working with Kaiming was really eye-opening for me, especially on how much care goes into a paper beyond the research itself. For him, writing isn't the last step you rush through before the deadline. It's part of the research. He'll go through a draft again and again, sometimes rewriting the same paragraph many times, until every sentence is doing real work.

The biggest thing I took away is that a paper should be easy to read. Not in a dumbed-down way, but in the sense that the reader shouldn't have to struggle to understand what you did and why it matters. Kaiming thinks a lot about the reader. What's the one message of this paper? Is the first figure telling that story? If someone only reads the abstract and looks at Figure 1, do they get it? That kind of discipline forces you to be very clear about your own idea. If you can't explain it simply, maybe you don't understand it well enough yet.

He also cares a lot about the details people might think are cosmetic: how a table is laid out, which numbers are bolded, whether the terminology stays consistent, whether a figure has unnecessary clutter. At first I thought, is this really that important? But over time I realized these things add up. They signal rigor, and they build trust. When a reader sees that everything is carefully done, they're more willing to believe your experiments too.

So now with my own students, I try to pass that on. I tell them the paper is the product. People won't run your code first. They'll read your paper, and that's the first impression of your work. Of course I'm not as patient as Kaiming, nobody is, but I hold a much higher bar than I would have otherwise. I'd rather we spend an extra week making the paper clean and honest than put out something that's messy and hard to follow. In the long run, I think that's how good work actually gets understood and has impact.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest thing I took from Kaiming is that a paper isn't finished when the experiments are done. It's finished when a reader can understand the idea without working hard for it. When we were writing ResNeXt together, I remember he would go over the same paragraph many, many times, and each pass the sentences got shorter and the figures got cleaner. At first I honestly thought it was a bit excessive. Later I realized that he was treating the presentation as part of the research itself, not as packaging.

He has this instinct for finding the one simple statement that captures the contribution. If you can't say what the paper is about in a sentence or two, then maybe you don't fully understand it yet. That changed how I think. Now, before I start writing, I ask myself what the single message is, and whether every figure and every table serves that message. If something is there just to show we did a lot of work, it usually gets cut.

The other thing is his attention to the first page. The abstract, the introduction, Figure 1. He believes most readers only see those, so they have to be nearly perfect. I've carried that into my own group. I tell my students that we will spend a surprising amount of time on Figure 1, and they should not be surprised when I ask for the tenth revision of a plot. It's not about being picky. It's respect for the reader's time, and a kind of honesty. A clear paper makes it easy for people to see exactly what you did and judge it fairly.

So I would say my standard now is simplicity, and I owe a lot of that to him. I'm probably still not as patient as Kaiming, but I try.

astra-6.text:
I think what I learned from Kaiming is that polishing a paper is really part of polishing the thinking. It’s not just making the English smoother or making a figure look nicer. It’s asking: What exactly are we trying to say? Is this claim supported by the experiment? Does the reader have enough context to understand why this matters?

That has really shaped my own standards. When you’ve worked on a project for a long time, everything feels obvious to you. But the reader doesn’t have that history. You have to build a clear path for them. And if a paragraph is very difficult to explain clearly, sometimes that means the idea itself still needs work. So I see presentation as part of the research, rather than something you do after the research is finished.

sol-6.1.text: What I learned from Kaiming is that polishing a paper is really about polishing your thinking. If you can’t explain something clearly, sometimes it means you haven’t understood it deeply enough yourself. It’s not just making the English sound better; it’s asking whether the motivation is clear, whether the evidence supports the claim, and whether a figure actually helps the reader understand the idea. That has pushed me to hold my own papers to a higher standard—to keep revising until the story is simple and precise, without making it stronger than the results justify.
